images.title: Every array of 18 tiles
images.purpose: Show that laying 18 tiles in equal rows gives three arrays, 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6, and that the numbers in them are the factors of 18.
images.composition: Three arrays of square tiles stacked in three bands, each with its multiplication to the right, and the list of factors along the bottom.
images.exact_structure: Plain white frame, 1456 by 816. At the top, centred at x 728 and y 60, the heading Arrays of 18 tiles in dark #1F2937 bold sans-serif (44 px). Below it exactly 3 arrays of square tiles, 18 tiles in each (54 tiles in all), every tile 44 by 44 px with a thin dark #2B2B2B outline and 6 px between tiles. ARRAY 1: 1 row of 18 tiles, filled teal #0072B2, x 100 to 994 and y 130 to 174. ARRAY 2: 2 rows of 9 tiles, filled amber #E69F00, x 100 to 544 and y 250 to 344. ARRAY 3: 3 rows of 6 tiles, filled reddish purple #CC79A7, x 100 to 394 and y 430 to 574. To the right of each array, left aligned and vertically centred on it, its multiplication in dark #1F2937 bold (44 px): 1 × 18 = 18 at x 1040 and y 152; 2 × 9 = 18 at x 600 and y 297; 3 × 6 = 18 at x 450 and y 502. At the bottom, centred at x 728 and y 700, the line Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18 in bold dark (50 px). No other text and no numbers inside the tiles. Nothing else in the frame.

images.takeaway: Each array of 18 tiles is a multiplication, and the numbers in the arrays, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18, are the factors of 18.
images.description: The arrays of 18 tiles: 1 row of 18, 2 rows of 9 and 3 rows of 6, each written as a multiplication, with the factors of 18 listed.
images.context: Concept image for Arrays Show Factors. It follows the idea of the array pictures in your maths book (a number of tiles in equal rows, written as a multiplication) and uses this concept's own example, 18 tiles.
images.teaching_notes: Count the tiles of each array together: all three have 18. The slip to watch is stopping at one array and missing the factors 1 and 18.

image_decisions.why: The arrays of 18 tiles make every pair of factors countable, which words alone do not.
